narrative_idea_gen: In the autumn of 1878, Eldon Krebs—the only licensed dentist west of Dodge City—spends a quiet week extracting teeth, adjusting plates, and privately reconciling the fact that he has been diluting his ether supply with lamp oil for three months, not because he can't afford more, but because he has grown to prefer the muffled, animal sounds his patients make when the anesthesia doesn't fully take. The story follows Eldon through mundane consultations, polite dinners with the pastor's wife, and his nightly habit of cataloging each extracted tooth in a leather journal with notes on the patient's scream pitch, all while the Kansas prairie outside his window offers no moral framework whatsoever—just wind and grass and the absolute indifference of geography. He is not a villain; he pays his taxes, feeds stray dogs, and is genuinely confused by the warmth he feels when a farmer's daughter thanks him through a swollen, bleeding mouth. The narrative drifts omnisciently from Eldon's careful hands to the thoughts of the town that considers him its most civilized citizen, building toward no climax at all—only the small, shattering moment when Eldon reorders his ether supply correctly, feels nothing about the decision, and understands that this, too, tells him nothing about himself.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for "The Dentist West of Dodge City"

---

## Beat 1: Eldon at Work — The Diluted Ether Introduced as Settled Fact

**Concrete Action:** Eldon performs a routine extraction in his small, well-kept office. We see his hands, his instruments, his procedure. The narration mentions, with neither emphasis nor apology, that he has been diluting his ether supply with lamp oil for three months. A patient groans through the procedure — not screaming, but not unconscious either. Eldon finishes, packs the wound, gives aftercare instructions. The patient thanks him. The day continues.

**Narrative Technique — Confession Disguised as Inventory:** The central horror of the story must be introduced with the same tonal weight as the layout of instruments on a tray. The omniscient narration should catalog the contents of Eldon's office — the ether bottle, the forceps, the porcelain bowl, the lamp oil — as items of equal status. The dilution is not revealed as a secret uncovered; it is presented as one fact among many in the accounting of a professional's day. The monstrous detail must arrive syntactically nested inside the mundane, the way Carver nested the wife's suicide attempt inside a dependent clause. The reader should have to double back: *wait, what did I just read?* The narration's refusal to flinch is the first indication that the story's moral universe operates under unfamiliar rules.

**Why This Beat Must Come First:** The story cannot work if the ether dilution is treated as a reveal. It is not a twist; it is a premise. Introducing it immediately — and flatly — tells the reader what kind of story this is: one in which the problem is not discovering the secret but living inside the consciousness that doesn't experience it as a secret. Everything that follows will be colored by this knowledge, and the reader's escalating discomfort will have to coexist with the story's absolute refusal to share that discomfort. The gap between reader and narrative tone *is* the engine. Establish it on the first page.

---

## Beat 2: The Town Perceives Its Most Civilized Citizen

**Concrete Action:** The omniscient narration lifts out of Eldon's office and surveys the town's relationship to him. We learn how Ford Bend regards its only dentist: the schoolteacher who recommends him to nervous children, the dry-goods merchant who considers him a peer in respectability, the women who note that he keeps a clean porch. Small, concrete moments — a nod on the street, a casserole left on his step after he treated a rancher's abscess for free — accumulate into a portrait of social esteem. Eldon pays his taxes. Eldon feeds stray dogs. Eldon is the man you want in your town.

**Narrative Technique — Omniscient Choral Voice as Ironic Counterweight:** This is where the omniscient point of view earns its structural necessity. The story needs a voice that can move through the town's collective consciousness — not any single townsperson, but the ambient, agreed-upon *reputation* of Eldon Krebs. This choral voice should feel warm, civic, approving. It should read almost like local history, the kind of thing that would appear in a county remembrance book. The technique is dramatic irony at the communal scale: an entire town's confident misreading of a man, delivered in language that is sincere on its own terms. No winking. No undercutting. The town is not stupid; it is simply working with the information available, which is all surfaces — and the surfaces are genuinely good.

**Why This Beat Matters Here:** Placed immediately after the ether revelation, this beat creates the story's defining structural tension: the simultaneity of two truths that cannot be reconciled by any character within the narrative. Eldon is a good citizen *and* a man who prefers his patients in pain. The town's wholehearted embrace of the first truth makes the second truth more disturbing, not less, because it demonstrates how completely competence and civility can conceal — or perhaps *coexist with* — something unnameable. This beat also prevents the reader from taking the easy exit of seeing Eldon as a hidden monster. He is not hiding. He is simply not legible, even to himself.

---

## Beat 3: Dinner with the Pastor's Wife — The Social Performance Sustained Without Effort

**Concrete Action:** Eldon dines at the home of Pastor Alden and his wife, Cordelia. The meal is modest, pleasant. Cordelia asks about his work, and Eldon responds with appropriate modesty and gentle humor. He compliments the food. He listens to the pastor discuss the challenges of a new church roof. Eldon offers to contribute. The conversation is warm, unremarkable, and utterly real — there is no moment in which Eldon feels like he is pretending. He enjoys the meal. He is good company. He walks home under stars.

**Narrative Technique — The Unsettling Power of Authentic Decency Performed by a Compromised Figure:** The dinner scene must resist every impulse toward subtext-as-menace. Eldon is not performing civility while secretly seething or fantasizing. He is genuinely present, genuinely kind, genuinely interested in the church roof. The omniscient narration should enter Cordelia's perspective just enough to confirm that she finds him pleasant and trustworthy — this is not a case of a woman sensing something "off." The technique is anti-suspense: giving the reader a scene in which the character they *know* to be disturbing behaves in ways that are not disturbing at all, and letting the dissonance do all the work. The horror is not that Eldon is faking; the horror is that he is not.

**Why This Beat Is Essential:** This scene establishes that Eldon's goodness and his cruelty occupy the same body without apparent friction. It forecloses the comforting interpretation that he is a sociopath wearing a mask. The dinner must be *pleasant to read* — the prose should slow down, become almost companionable. The reader should catch themselves relaxing into the scene and then feel the floor shift: *I am enjoying an evening with a man who dilutes his patients' anesthesia.* The beat forces complicity. It also anchors the story in the specific social texture of 1878 frontier Kansas — the pastor's wife, the church roof, the walk under stars — grounding the moral problem in a world that feels fully inhabited rather than schematic.

---

## Beat 4: The Journal — Eldon Catalogs His Extractions by Scream Pitch

**Concrete Action:** Late at night, after the dinner, Eldon sits at his desk with a leather-bound journal. We watch him make his entries. Each extracted tooth is logged: patient name, tooth number, date, condition. Alongside these clinical details, in the same careful handwriting, he notes the quality and pitch of the sound the patient made during extraction. The notations are precise, almost musical — he has developed a personal vocabulary for this. He writes with the same diligence he gives to everything. He does not appear agitated or aroused. He closes the journal, places it in a drawer, and prepares for bed.

**Narrative Technique — The Private Ritual Rendered Without Psychological Explanation:** This is the scene the reader has been dreading, and Carver's principle applies in inverted form: where Carver withheld interiority to let the reader fill the gap with understanding, this story must withhold interiority to let the reader fill the gap with *dread*. The omniscient narration should describe the journaling with the same meticulous, uninflected attention it gave to the dinner conversation. No access to why Eldon does this. No language of compulsion, pleasure, shame, or ritual. Just a man writing in a notebook before bed. The specific notations — the vocabulary he has invented for gradations of sound — should be rendered in enough detail to feel real and systematic, but not so much that it becomes Grand Guignol. The restraint is everything. The reader must be given just enough rope to hang their own interpretation on.

**Why This Beat Must Follow the Dinner:** The sequencing is the argument. Dinner with the pastor's wife, then scream-pitch journaling, then bed — all with the same emotional temperature. The juxtaposition is the point, but it must not feel like juxtaposition; it must feel like routine. If the story has done its work, the reader will arrive at this scene already destabilized by the dinner's normalcy and will find the journal scene destabilizing for the opposite reason: because it, too, feels normal. The journal is also the story's most concrete emblem of the problem — Eldon is a man who catalogs experience rather than feeling it, who converts the sounds of suffering into data. He is, in his own way, as sealed inside a system of recording as Carver's narrator was sealed inside his reductive language. But unlike the narrator of "Cathedral," no Robert is coming to break the seal.

---

## Beat 5: The Farmer's Daughter — Warmth Eldon Cannot Locate

**Concrete Action:** A young woman, a farmer's daughter, comes in with an abscessed molar. Eldon extracts it. The diluted ether leaves her semi-conscious — she grips the chair, makes sounds, endures. Afterward, her mouth packed and swollen, she looks up at Eldon and thanks him with evident, uncomplicated gratitude. She means it. Eldon feels warmth — genuine warmth — and is confused by it. He does not know whether the warmth is a response to her gratitude, to her pain, to her youth, to some combination, or to something else entirely. The narration registers his confusion and does not resolve it. She leaves. He stands in his office and does not move for a while.

**Narrative Technique — The Interior Close-Up That Reveals the Absence of Self-Knowledge:** This is the one moment where the omniscient narration moves fully into Eldon's consciousness and *stays*, and what it finds is not malice or lust or sadism but genuine bewilderment. The technique is the anti-epiphany staged as almost-epiphany: Eldon feels something true, reaches toward understanding, and finds nothing. The narration should slow to near-stillness here, the prose rhythm shifting to shorter sentences, more pauses, imitating the halting quality of a mind trying and failing to read itself. The farmer's daughter should be rendered with great specificity — her hands, the mud on her boots, the particular quality of her voice through the packing — so that she exists as a full person in the scene, not merely as a catalyst for Eldon's inner life. Her gratitude must feel real and unironic; she is genuinely thankful to the man who hurt her more than he needed to.

**Why This Beat Is the Emotional Crux:** This is the scene that makes Eldon human in the most discomforting way possible. A villain who enjoys pain is a known quantity; a man who cannot tell whether he enjoys pain, or kindness, or simply the proximity of another person's unguarded body — that is something the reader has no ready category for. The warmth is real. The confusion is real. And the impossibility of sorting one from the other is the story's deepest claim about the opacity of the self. This beat is analogous to the moment in "Cathedral" when the narrator admits "cathedrals don't mean anything special to me" — it is the most honest thing Eldon experiences, and it provides no relief. The farmer's daughter functions as the story's one point of pure, undefended human contact, and the fact that it occurs across an asymmetry of power and pain is what makes it unbearable.

---

## Beat 6: The Prairie — Geography as Moral Silence

**Concrete Action:** Eldon stands at his window at night, or walks to the edge of town, and looks at the Kansas prairie. Wind, grass, stars, the long dark line of the horizon. The narration expands outward — this is the most sweeping, lyrical passage in the story. We leave Eldon's body and survey the landscape: the emptiness that goes on for days in every direction, the indifference of the physical world. There is no church steeple visible. There is no neighboring town's light. There is only flatness. Eldon stands in it or looks at it, and the narration lets the silence extend.

**Narrative Technique — Landscape as the Refusal of Moral Scaffolding:** Where "Cathedral" used the television documentary to introduce an object dense with spiritual meaning (the cathedral, centuries of faith made physical), this story uses the prairie to introduce the *absence* of that scaffolding. The prose should be detailed and beautiful — Carver's minimalism will not serve here; the landscape passage needs enough lyricism to make the reader feel the size and emptiness — but the beauty must be cold. This is nature as amoral fact. The technique is a kind of negative sublime: awe without God, grandeur without implication. The narration should explicitly note, or allow the reader to feel, that the prairie offers Eldon no judgment, no reflection, no framework for understanding what he is. It is not hostile. It is not indifferent in a cruel way. It is simply *there*, the way Eldon is simply there
narrative_story:
# The Dentist West of Dodge City

## I.

The office of Eldon Krebs occupied the ground floor of a clapboard building on Ford Bend's main street, between Havershaw's dry-goods store and the lot where Dunlap kept his farrier's equipment under a canvas lean-to. The building had been a land office before the railroad survey shifted south and took the speculators with it, and Eldon had purchased it in the spring of 1876 for forty dollars and a promise to maintain the exterior. He had kept the promise. The porch boards were sound, the steps were swept, and the shingle hung straight: E. KREBS, D.D.S. — EXTRACTIONS, FILINGS, PLATES. The letters had been painted by Eldon himself, in a blue that matched the particular shade favored by the College of Dental Surgery in Cincinnati, where he had studied for two years before heading west.

Inside, the office was twelve feet by fourteen. A Ritter operating chair, purchased secondhand from a retiring practitioner in Wichita, sat in the center of the room. Beside it, a small oak table held the instruments in their proper order: the extraction forceps — upper universal, lower bicuspid, cowhorn for molars — the elevators, the scalers, the mouth mirror, a porcelain bowl for spit and blood, cotton wadding in a glass jar, and a brown bottle of ether with a folded cloth beside it. Along the far wall stood a cabinet with three drawers, the top two holding supplies, the bottom one locked. A window with a cotton curtain let in eastern light. The floor was pine, sanded and sealed, and Eldon mopped it with lye water each evening. There was no carpet. Carpet held what a dentist's floor collected, and Eldon did not believe in holding what ought to be cleaned away.

On this morning in October of 1878, the man in the Ritter chair was Gerald Parkins, a teamster who hauled goods between Ford Bend and the railroad depot at Cimarron. Parkins was forty-one, thick through the shoulders, and frightened. His right lower second molar had cracked along the root, and the gum around it had gone scarlet and hot, and for six days he had packed the socket with clove-soaked cotton and drunk whiskey until the pain became merely the loudest thing in the room rather than the only thing. Now the clove had stopped working and the whiskey had run out and Parkins sat with his mouth open and his fingers white on the chair's armrests while Eldon examined the tooth with a probe.

"Root's split clean through," Eldon said. "No saving it, Mr. Parkins. We'll have it out."

Parkins nodded. He had nodded before Eldon finished the sentence, the way they always did when the pain had become a residency rather than a visit.

Eldon folded the cloth into a cone and uncapped the brown bottle. For three months he had been replacing what he used from the bottle with lamp oil — not all at once, but steadily, a ratio he adjusted by instinct rather than measurement, so that the ether that wet the cloth was now more than half kerosene by volume. He held the cloth over Parkins's nose and mouth. "Breathe as deep as you can, now. Slow and deep."

Parkins breathed. His eyes stayed open. They drifted, fogged somewhat, but did not close. Eldon watched the muscles in the man's jaw slacken partially, a loosening that resembled sleep the way a sketch resembles its subject. He set the cloth aside and selected the cowhorn forceps.

The extraction took ninety seconds. Parkins groaned throughout — a sustained, guttural sound, the body's low protest lodged somewhere beneath whatever diminished consciousness the ether had left him. His hands clenched and released. His boots scraped the footrest. At one point a sound came from his throat that was higher than the groan, sharper, a brief bright note that broke through the murk of the anesthetic like a bird breaking the surface of water, and then it was over. Eldon held the fractured molar up to the light, examined the roots — both pieces, cleanly split, no fragments left behind — and placed it in the porcelain bowl.

"That's done," he said.

He packed the socket with cotton and oil of cloves — real cloves, full strength; Eldon did not economize with aftercare — and gave Parkins instructions: no chewing on that side, salt rinses twice a day, return in a week or sooner if the bleeding would not stop. Parkins stood carefully, one hand on the chair. His face was damp and pale but already reorganizing itself around the relief of aftermath. The pain of the last six days was gone. What remained was the fresh, clean ache of a wound that would heal.

"Thank you, Doc," Parkins said, or tried to say; the packing made it indistinct. He put two silver dollars on the oak table.

"One is sufficient," Eldon said.

"Take both. You earned it."

Eldon took both. He walked Parkins to the door, watched him descend the porch steps into the morning light, and returned to his office. He emptied the porcelain bowl, rinsed it, wiped the forceps with alcohol, and replaced each instrument in its position on the tray. Then he mopped the area around the chair, though there was little to mop. It had been a clean extraction. Most of his extractions were clean. Whatever else could be said about the practice of Eldon Krebs, his technique was meticulous, his hands were steady, and his patients kept their appointments.

He stood at the window for a moment, watching the street. A dog trotted past. The morning was cool and dry, the sky a pale even blue that would deepen by noon. He had two more patients scheduled before midday and another in the afternoon, a child with a milk tooth that had abscessed and whose mother had been told by the schoolteacher that Dr. Krebs was gentle with children and it would be all right.

He returned to his instruments and began to lay out what he would need for the next procedure.

---

## II.

The town of Ford Bend had existed for eleven years and had been incorporated for three. It sat on the north bank of a creek that fed the Arkansas River somewhere to the southeast, in a stretch of country where the shortgrass prairie began to give way to the sandhills and the wind came from the west with nothing to break it for two hundred miles. It was not Dodge City. The people of Ford Bend said this often and meant it as a point of pride. Dodge City, twenty-six miles to the east, had its cattle trade and its railroad and its famous sheriff and its famous violence and its women whose names appeared in newspapers as far away as Chicago, and Ford Bend wanted none of it. Ford Bend wanted a schoolhouse, which it had. A church, which it had, though the roof leaked. A general store, a post office, a blacksmith, and a dentist.

It had a dentist.

There was general agreement, among the families who had settled in Ford Bend and the ranchers who used it as their supply town and the drovers who occasionally passed through on their way to somewhere more exciting, that Eldon Krebs was one of the better things the town had going for it. Not the best thing — that was the water, which came from a good well and had no alkali taste — but close. He had arrived in the spring of 1876 with a wagonload of equipment, a certificate from a genuine dental college, and a manner so quiet and steady that people trusted him before they had any evidence that they should. The evidence came soon enough. He fixed what could be fixed, pulled what couldn't, and charged fairly. He did not drink. He did not gamble. He attended church, though he sat in the back and did not sing. He paid his property tax on time and had once, without being asked, repaired the hinge on the schoolhouse gate.

Clara Havershaw, the dry-goods merchant's wife, kept a clean-porch index in her mind — a private ranking of the town's residents by the maintenance of their front stoops — and Eldon Krebs had occupied the top position since the week he arrived. She said so to her husband, who repeated it in the store, and it became one of those small facts that circulate through a town until they are no longer gossip but geography: *Krebs keeps a clean porch.* It meant more than a clean porch. It meant a man you could rely on, a citizen of the type that towns needed if they were going to remain towns and not dissolve back into prairie at the first hard winter.

The schoolteacher, Miss Addie Parsons, recommended Dr. Krebs to every child who came to school crying with a toothache, which happened often enough that she had developed a standard speech. "Dr. Krebs is very gentle," she would say, kneeling before whatever small, ruined face had appeared at her desk that morning. "He will explain everything he is going to do before he does it, and it will be over very quickly, and afterward your mouth will feel so much better that you will wonder why you waited." She believed this fully. She had been his patient herself — a cracked filling, replaced without incident — and she had found him calm, attentive, and precise. The fact that she had felt more of the procedure than she expected she attributed to her own low tolerance for discomfort, a personal failing she had always suspected and now felt confirmed.

A rancher named Elias Coombs had, the previous winter, developed an abscess so severe that the left side of his face swelled to the size and color of a ripe plum, and he had ridden nine miles through sleet to reach Eldon's office. Eldon drained the abscess, extracted the tooth, and kept Coombs in the operating chair for two hours while the bleeding slowed, feeding him sips of water and speaking to him in a low, even voice about the habits of pronghorn antelope, which Coombs found interesting and later said had kept him from panicking. Eldon charged him one dollar. Coombs's wife sent a casserole the following week — salt pork and beans and dried corn, in a Dutch oven she expected returned — and after that, the Coombs family did not go to any other dentist, though the nearest alternative was in Dodge City and by some accounts better equipped.

People greeted Eldon on the street and he greeted them back. He tipped his hat to women. He stopped to speak to children. He had once carried three sacks of flour from Havershaw's store to the church kitchen for the pastor's wife without being asked, simply because he was passing when the delivery arrived and she was standing in the doorway looking at the sacks with the expression of a woman calculating the distance between where the flour was and where the flour needed to be. He did not court anyone, which some of the women in town found regrettable and others found suspicious, but most found simply consistent with the rest of him: a man of deep domestic order who had, perhaps, ordered himself so thoroughly that there was no room left over for the disorder that courtship required.

He fed the stray dogs that gathered behind the buildings on the west end of town. Not lavishly — scraps, put out in a tin plate each evening, retrieved and washed each morning. The dogs came to know his schedule and would be sitting in a loose group behind his building as the light failed, and he would come out with the plate and set it down and stand for a moment watching them eat, and then go inside. He did not name them. He did not pet them. But he fed them, and they were fed, and in Ford Bend this was known and counted.

---

## III.

Pastor Alden and his wife, Cordelia, lived in a three-room house attached to the back of the church by a covered walkway that leaked in the same places the church roof leaked, so that on rainy Sundays the pastor arrived at his pulpit already damp. They had been in Ford Bend for four years. They had no children. They had a garden that produced squash, and they had each other, and they had a habit of inviting someone to dinner every Thursday, which Cordelia said was for fellowship and Alden said was to keep them from going strange, the way couples did when they talked only to each other for too long.

On this Thursday, the guest was Eldon.

He arrived at six with a small jar of honey he had purchased from a beekeeper outside of Cimarron, and Cordelia accepted it with the genuine delight of a woman for whom honey was not routine. The table was set with three places, a cloth that had been white before the Kansas dust got to it, and dishes that did not match but were clean and unchipped. Dinner was jackrabbit stew with carrots and the last of the garden's squash, biscuits made with lard, and coffee that had been boiled twice because Alden believed second-boiled coffee had more character, a position Cordelia disputed but had stopped arguing.

"This is very good, Mrs. Alden," Eldon said, and he meant it. The stew was good. The biscuits were good. The coffee was terrible in a way that was familiar and therefore comforting, and he drank two cups.

"Cordelia," she said. "I have told you. If we are to eat together, you will call me Cordelia."

"Cordelia," Eldon said, and smiled, and the smile was small and real.

The conversation moved where Thursday-dinner conversation moved: to the church roof, which had been leaking since spring; to the cost of lumber, which had risen; to the question of whether the congregation could raise the money by subscription or whether someone would need to write to the mission board in Topeka, which Alden considered humiliating and Cordelia considered practical. Eldon listened with his head slightly tilted, the way he listened to patients describing their symptoms — close attention that did not interrupt.

"I would like to contribute," Eldon said, when Alden paused. "Toward the roof."

"That is generous, Eldon, but —"

"Ten dollars," Eldon said. "It is not enough to fix it, but it is enough to begin."

Alden looked at his wife. Cordelia looked at Eldon. Ten dollars was not a small amount. It was five extractions, or ten fillings, or one month's rent on the building that housed his practice. Eldon knew this. He offered it the way he offered everything — quietly, without ceremony, as if the decision had been made before the conversation and the conversation was merely the mechanism by which it reached the world.

"We are grateful," Cordelia said.

"The roof should not leak on a man while he is trying to preach," Eldon said, and this was a joke, or near enough to one, and they laughed, and the evening continued.

Alden spoke about a family homesteading to the northwest who had lost a child to scarlet fever, and about his visit to them, and about the difficulty of offering comfort when comfort was not, strictly speaking, available. Eldon listened. He asked how the family was managing for food, and when Alden said they were managing poorly, Eldon said he would put together a package from Havershaw's and have it sent. This was the kind of thing Eldon did. It was not calculated. It arose from the same place in him that fed the dogs and carried the flour and kept the porch swept — some interior mechanism of order and responsibility that operated as continuously and unthinkingly as a heartbeat.

Cordelia, watching him across the table as he spoke with her husband about the bereaved family's provisions, thought, not for the first time, that Eldon Krebs was the kind of man who made a town feel like a town. There were men who extracted resources from a place — the cattlemen, the speculators — and men who deposited something into it, some ballast of reliability that kept the whole enterprise from blowing away. Eldon was the second kind. She trusted him the way she trusted the well water: deeply, automatically, without the need for continuous reassessment. There was nothing in his manner that gave her pause. There was nothing in his eyes that she needed to look away from. He was simply a good man whose company was pleasant, and she was glad he had come to dinner, and she told him so as he put on his hat at the door.

"It has been a fine evening," Eldon said. "Thank you, Cordelia. Pastor."

"Walk safe," Alden said.

"Always do."

He walked home through the dark. The street was empty, the buildings closed, the sky enormous and cloudless, salted with stars so dense and bright that they seemed almost to have texture, as if the sky were not a void but a surface. The air smelled of grass and cold and the distant ghost of woodsmoke from someone's stove. His boots sounded on the packed dirt of the street, then on the boards of his porch, then on the pine floor of his office. He lit a lamp. He hung his hat. He stood for a moment
narrative_idea_gen_original_prompt:
Prison Strings

Jolyne Cujoh & Makima

Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is.

**Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)**
Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive.
Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!"

**Makima (Chainsaw Man)**
Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly.
Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners."

Third person, present tense.

Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Length: 1000 words.
